analysis.one_liner: Narrows the legal immunity that shields social media platforms from lawsuits over third-party content.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee from referral in February 2023 until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Section 230 of the Communications Act gives websites and social media platforms broad immunity from lawsuits over what other people post. This bill would punch holes in that shield: platforms could be sued over paid content or content they helped create, victims of online stalking and harassment, discrimination, and wrongful death could sue, courts could order platforms to remove harmful material, and platforms would have to prove in court that the immunity applies to them. It was introduced by Rep. Kathy Castor with two Democratic cosponsors and never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: People harmed online — targets of stalking, harassment, and intimidation; people facing discriminatory conduct on platforms; victims of scams in paid content; civil rights plaintiffs; antitrust enforcers; and families pursuing wrongful death claims — would gain the ability to hold platforms accountable in court.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Victims of online harassment and discrimination

how_it_helps.text: The bill would remove immunity where a platform 'accepted payment to make the speech available' or created or funded the content, opening paid advertising, sponsored content, and platform-produced material to ordinary liability [S2] [S3].
It would expressly exempt civil rights, antitrust, stalking and harassment, international human rights, and wrongful death claims from the Section 230 shield, allowing victims to sue [S2] [S3].

It would let courts issue injunctions ordering platforms to remove or restrict material likely to cause irreparable harm, while protecting platforms from liability for complying with such orders [S2] [S3].
It would make Section 230 an affirmative defense the defendant must prove, shifting the burden from plaintiffs to platforms [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Internet platforms and social media companies would bear more lawsuits, litigation costs, and court-ordered content removals; some of those costs would likely be passed to users through tighter moderation and fewer services.

drawbacks.text: Narrowing Section 230 could push platforms to remove far more material, including lawful and valuable speech, rather than risk litigation — the core criticism that shaped Section 230's original design. The bill's expansion of liability for paid content would also reach advertising-funded services broadly [S2] [S3].

Defendants would bear the burden of proving the immunity applies, raising the cost of defending even strong cases and potentially deterring small platforms and startups that cannot absorb litigation [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real recourse to people the current law often leaves without remedy — harassment victims, discrimination plaintiffs, and scam targets — and its injunction carve-out is designed to protect platforms that comply with court orders. The trade-off is genuine: broader liability tends to produce aggressive over-removal of user speech and heavier compliance costs that weigh hardest on smaller platforms. Whether the courts could handle the resulting litigation without chilling legitimate online speech is the honest objection to the design.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Innovation, Data, and Commerce Subcommittee in early 2023, and the committee never took it up before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Kathy Castor (D-FL) introduced the SAFE TECH Act on February 28, 2023, with Rep. Andy Levin, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1] [S3] [S5].
Two Democratic cosponsors joined the bill; no Republican cosponsored [S4].
On March 10, 2023, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce, where it remained; there is no record of a markup, hearing action, or floor vote [S5].
The bill's only action for the remainder of the 118th Congress was that subcommittee referral — it died at the end of the Congress on January 3, 2025 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Internet platforms are better off: they keep the broad Section 230 immunity intact, while harassment victims, discrimination plaintiffs, and people scammed through paid content remain without a path to sue. Supporters of stronger platform accountability gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Internet platforms keeping their legal shield

for.name: Rep. Kathy Castor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to narrow Section 230's platform immunity for civil rights, victims' rights, and consumer protections.

for.name: Rep. Andy Levin
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or advanced the bill out of committee in nearly two years.

against.name: Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 10, 2023 and took no further action on record.

against.name: Rep. Cathy McMorris Rodgers
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair during the 118th Congress, never brought the bill to a markup or floor consideration.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the only recorded support came from three House Democrats, and the committee that controlled the bill's fate was under Republican leadership, so the partisan shape can only be inferred from the absence of Republican cosponsors.

industries.note: The bill would strip away much of the Section 230 immunity that protects platforms from lawsuits over third-party content, exposing them to civil rights, antitrust, harassment, and wrongful death suits and court-ordered takedowns. Platforms' interest in preserving that shield runs against users seeking recourse for harms suffered online.

industries.industry: Advertising-funded online services and ad tech
industries.note: The carve-out for content a platform is 'paid to make available' would pull most paid advertising and sponsored content out from under the immunity shield, expanding litigation exposure across the ad-supported internet.
Making Section 230 an affirmative defense the platform must prove would raise litigation costs that fall hardest on small businesses without large legal departments.
